articles.title: Archaeologists found 9,000-year-old arrowheads covered in strange markings; their purpose remains a mystery
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For nearly nine thousand years, a set of Anatolian arrowheads has been quietly guarding a secret. Archaeologists working at Tepecik-Ciftlik, a Neolith.
articles.body: For nearly nine thousand years, a set of Anatolian arrowheads has been quietly guarding a secret. Archaeologists working at Tepecik-Ciftlik, a Neolithic settlement in Cappadocia, central Turkey, have identified eleven newly recognised obsidian points bearing deliberate, hand-cut incisions, bringing the site's total to twelve and the wider regional count to 54. According to the study published in PLOS One, titled ‘Intentional incisions on Neolithic Obsidian arrowheads from Central Anatolia: A techno-functional and iconographic approach’, these markings were made on purpose, not left by accident during manufacture or centuries buried in the ground. Yet despite careful microscopic analysis, experimental replication and comparison with dozens of similar finds across Central Anatolia, the arrowheads' meaning remains stubbornly out of reach. Were they hunters' signatures, decorative flourishes, or something closer to ritual? No two designs match, and the practice never spread beyond this one corner of the ancient world, leaving researchers with more questions than answers.9,000-year-old Neolithic arrowheads in Turkey show mysterious incised symbolsThese arrowheads are not distinguished by their shape or size, which match the ordinary points found alongside them, but by the presence of small, hand-cut lines etched into their ventral faces, crosses, chevrons, wavy lines, squares, and an occasional letter-like form. Microscopic examination ruled out accidental scratching. The researchers established three criteria for genuine incisions, namely visibility to the naked eye, clear removal of material, and evidence of repeated, controlled strokes, and on that basis confirmed intentional marks on ten of the twelve pieces, with two remaining ambiguous.No two designs are identical, and the number of strokes required ranges from a single cut to twenty on the most elaborate specimen, arrowhead 4, whose three linked squares took repeated passes to complete. The corpus shows "no correlation with raw material, chaîne opératoire, typology, or use-wear." In other words, whatever drove someone to mark a particular point, it wasn't linked to how the tool was made or used.Flint tools were used to carve markings into obsidian arrowheadsTo understand the technique, the team ran an experiment, attempting to incise a fresh obsidian blade with both a flint tool and another piece of obsidian. Obsidian proved too soft to mark obsidian effectively, whereas a flint edge, harder on the Mohs scale, cut clean, deliberate lines. That is notable because flint makes up under one per cent of the site's stone tools, suggesting its use here was a considered choice rather than convenience.The timing of the incisions relative to each arrowhead's shaping proved just as inconsistent as everything else. In three cases the cuts were made before the final retouching, in three others afterwards, and in six the sequence could not be determined at all. Functionally, the picture is similarly murky: only one incised point, arrowhead 11, showed a fracture consistent with having struck a target, while the rest bore no clear signs of use as projectiles, ruling neither hunting nor purely symbolic purposes in or out.Why Neolithic communities in Turkey carved mysterious markings into arrowheadsThe mystery isn't confined to Tepecik-Ciftlik. Similar incised arrowheads have turned up at Çatalhöyük, Can Hasan III, Kömürcü-Kaletepe and a handful of other Cappadocian and Konya Plain sites, and the study notes intriguing formal echoes between them, such as a cross at Tepecik-Ciftlik resembling one from Çatalhöyük, and wavy-line motifs matching pieces from Can Hasan III. Yet Cappadocian obsidian itself travelled far beyond the region, as far as the southern Levant, without carrying the incising tradition with it, which the authors argue points to "specific cultural practices confined to certain Neolithic communities."The leading theory, first proposed by archaeologist Kathryn Ataman in 1988 after studying arrowheads from Can Hasan III, was that the marks functioned as hunters' signatures, a way of claiming a kill, drawing loosely on ethnographic parallels from Inuit hunting groups. Comparing the Anatolian finds against incised projectiles from Iron Age Phoenicia, Bronze Age Mesopotamia and Palaeolithic Europe turned up no close parallel, leading the pair to conclude only that decoration, ownership marks and something closer to ritual or magical practice all remain plausible.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Spain requests emergency funding from the EU over Ceuta migrants
articles.summary: European Commission says it is ‘assessing’ Spain’s request after some 70,000 migrants surged into North African enclave.
articles.body:
Spain has formally requested emergency funding from the European Union to address the migration situation in its North African enclave of Ceuta, weeks after tens of thousands of people surged across the border from Morocco.

The European Commission said on Tuesday that it is closely monitoring the situation and remained “fully engaged at all levels” to ensure the security of the EU’s external borders.

list 2 of 3 Moroccan police arrest over 100 migrants trying to reach Spanish enclave

list 3 of 3 Hundreds of migrants arrested near Ceuta border in latest crackdown

Commission spokesman Markus Lammert said during a daily news briefing in Brussels, “We have now, namely yesterday, received a formal request for emergency funding, and we are now working on assessing their request as a priority and with a view to taking a swift decision.”

This comes after more than 70,000 would-be migrants, driven by poverty and misinformation, rushed towards Ceuta at the end of July, in one of the deadliest migration crises to hit the region.

At least 90 people died on both sides of the border, according to official numbers, while human rights groups reported higher figures.

The Spanish government also took steps to speed up the return of the migrants who still remain in the Spanish territory of Ceuta.

Most of them have since returned to Morocco, but between five percent and 10 percent – between 3,500 and 7,000 people – remain in Ceuta, including unaccompanied children who cannot be deported.

Spanish authorities must identify those remaining in Ceuta to establish whether they are entitled to international protection or, if not, begin procedures for their return.

The process has been criticised as too slow by Ceuta’s regional government, which is controlled by the conservative Popular Party (PP).

To speed up the response, Spain’s cabinet on Tuesday approved the creation of a “single command” for Ceuta, to be led by Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres.

The priority is “the return and repatriation of the greatest possible number of people, adults and minors”, while respecting Spanish law and human rights, Torres told reporters after the cabinet approved the measure.

While return procedures are accelerated, the government will continue to provide humanitarian assistance to those who seek asylum or are unaccompanied minors and therefore cannot be returned, he added.

Ceuta and Melilla, Spain’s two North African enclaves, hold the EU’s only land borders with Africa.

Both enclaves operate under a special arrangement within the Schengen free-travel zone, which requires anyone crossing in to face border checks before continuing onward to mainland Spain.

articles.title: Waymo robotaxis are headed to Munich | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Germany's autonomous vehicle regulations have made it a hotspot for autonomous vehicle testing and eventual commercial robotaxi deployment.
articles.body:
Waymo said Tuesday it plans to launch a robotaxi service in Munich, months after the Alphabet-owned autonomous vehicle company set up an entity in Germany.

The company still must weave its way through mapping and testing, as well as clear regulatory hurdles before it can launch commercial operations.

Waymo will begin, as it has in the other 11 cities where it has commercial robotaxi operations, by first manually driving its vehicles to map the streets of Munich. It will then test its autonomous vehicles with human safety drivers behind the wheel, before removing them. Waymo typically allows its employees, media, and other invited guests to ride in its driverless vehicles at this stage.

The company will eventually open its robotaxis to limited service, and eventually to all riders once it receives the regulatory approval required to operate commercially. Waymo said in a blog post on Tuesday that it is working with Germany’s Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA), state authorities, and local officials, and expects to open commercial ride-hailing to the public toward the end of 2027.

Waymo’s entry into Germany comes more than five years after the country’s lawmakers adopted legislation to allow driverless vehicles on public roads , and in that process making it the first country in the European Union to create a legal framework for Level 4 autonomous driving. Level 4 autonomy is a designation by the Society of Automobile Engineers (SAE) that means the self-driving system handles all the driving, with no expectation of a human taking over, in certain conditions or environments.

This legal framework has made Germany a hotspot for autonomous vehicle testing. Today, several companies, including Mobileye and Volkswagen, hold permits to test their autonomous vehicles in the country, according to the KBA’s latest data. Waymo does not currently have any permits.

However, the vast majority, including U.K. self-driving startup Wayve, and Israel-based Autobrains, hold Level 3 permits. Level 3, or conditional automated driving, is a system that can handle all the driving within specific operating conditions, such as low speeds on highways, but the driver must be able to take over when needed.

Germany isn’t the only overseas hotspot for AV developers. The U.K., especially London, is shaping up as another robotaxi battleground. Waymo has said it plans to launch a commercial service in London in 2026, which will pit it against Wayve and its partner Uber . Chinese tech giant Baidu has also started testing autonomous vehicles in the city as part of its partnership with Lyft and Freenow.

articles.title: Fatah, Dahlan bloc hold reconciliation talks ahead of Palestinian elections
articles.summary: Fatah and Dahlan’s Democratic Reform hold talks in Alamein as fears grow over a potential opposition coalition.
articles.body:
High-level delegations from the Fatah movement, which dominates the Palestinian Authority (PA), and influential former top official Mohammed Dahlan’s Democratic Reform bloc have convened in the Egyptian city of Alamein for critical reconciliation talks ahead of Palestinian legislative elections.

The meeting on Monday, publicised by Democratic Reform, comes as Fatah’s rivals – including Dahlan’s group and Hamas – discuss forming a broad coalition that could pose a significant challenge to the party in November’s elections.

Monday’s meetings were led by PA Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh, a senior Fatah official, and Democratic Reform’s deputy leader Samir al-Mashharawi.

Although al-Mashharawi described the initial atmosphere in Alamein as positive, he added that nothing “practical” had yet been agreed and said that PA President Mahmoud Abbas needed to make “decisive decisions” in order to unite the Fatah movement. Democratic Reform is largely made up of ex-Fatah officials who have broken away over differences with Abbas.

“Everyone who was subjected to unjust decisions inside the Fatah movement must have their rights returned,” al-Mashharawi said. He defended Democratic Reform’s recent dialogue with other Palestinian factions, saying that “any alliances in the upcoming elections do not target the Fatah movement or its leadership”.

Hamas official Husam Badran told Al Jazeera last week that the Palestinian group had met recently with officials from Democratic Reform – as well as Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine – with the aim of forming a national bloc to contest the elections, the first since 2006.

The meeting with Dahlan was notable because Hamas and the Democratic Reform leader were opponents in Gaza for years, during Dahlan’s time as one of Fatah’s most powerful officials in the enclave. That culminated in the 2007 conflict between Hamas and Fatah, which led to Fatah being forced out of Gaza.

The proposed anti-Fatah bloc has alarmed the movement’s leadership, and was the main driver behind Monday’s meeting, according to political analyst Ahmed al-Tanani.

“The main goal that the Fatah delegation came for is to neutralise the Dahlan participation in this alliance,” al-Tanani told Al Jazeera, adding that the prospect of a unified opposition “complicated Abbas’s calculations”.

Fatah’s attempt to prevent the coalition from forming highlights the dangers it presents. Any coalition would emphasise Fatah’s divisions, because Democratic Reform is a breakaway Fatah faction, and its members are still associated with the movement. It could also bring several disparate Palestinian factions together in a common challenge to the leadership of Abbas, who is now 90 years old and facing widespread opposition.

Gaza-based analyst Eyad al-Qarra said that a Dahlan-Hamas electoral coalition would allow Hamas to have more legitimacy to govern if it won, even after it announced that it was dissolving its administration in Gaza.

Dahlan would also be able to present himself in a positive light internationally.

“It is an attempt to present Dahlan and his faction to regional and international players as capable of achieving what Mahmoud Abbas could not – reaching serious understandings with Palestinian factions across the political spectrum,” al-Tanani said.

Given Abbas’s advanced age, there is also the question of Fatah’s succession planning, with Dahlan being presented among the possible names.

But al-Tanani said it was too early to suggest that Monday’s meeting could portend an improvement in Dahlan’s chances. He explained that absorbing Democratic Reform “would mean a widespread internal coup and a threat to the interests of the current leadership”.

Any reintegration of Dahlan would also spell bad news for other contenders for the PA leadership including Abbas’s son Yasser, who won a seat on Fatah’s Central Committee in May.

“If Dahlan comes in, Yasser’s chances will be bad,” al-Qarra said.

He added that current Fatah leaders were fearful of an alliance of dissenters within the movement, including Dahlan, the popular leader Marwan Barghouti – who is imprisoned by Israel – and Nasser al-Qudwa, a veteran politician.

Samih Khalaf, a Palestinian writer and a former member of Fatah, agreed that a return for Dahlan to Fatah would disrupt Yasser Abbas’s rise.

“The phenomenon of Dahlan poses a danger not only to an individual like the president, but also to the president’s preparations to pass down power to his son,” Khalaf said.

The problem for Yasser Abbas was that he would not be able to balance Dahlan’s influence if the latter returned to Fatah, Khalaf added.

Mahmoud Abbas has never publicly stated that he plans for Yasser Abbas to inherit the presidency.

International pressure has played into Abbas’s decision to return to the ballot box, after he repeatedly delayed elections for years.

The push for elections forms part of a wider reform agenda backed by European and Arab governments, including an initiative produced by France and Saudi Arabia to work towards a two-state solution.

“The main motive for the Authority going toward elections is primarily linked to a European path, or at least a Franco-Saudi path aligned with the European Union, aimed at pushing reforms,” al-Tanani said.

For Dahlan, however, elections could offer something more: a route back into formal Palestinian politics.

Al-Tanani said that elections presented Dahlan an opportunity to convert his continued influence – despite living in the United Arab Emirates for years – into formal political representation.

Dahlan “saw in the Palestinian elections a golden opportunity to re-establish himself within the official Palestinian political system”, al-Tanani said.

“Only the ballot box and the regional and international dimension may have the largest role in determining the shape of the political system and its future leadership,” he said.

That calculation also helps explain what analysts describe as Hamas’s increasingly pragmatic approach towards Dahlan.

“Hamas is being intelligent,” al-Qarra said. “It deals with everyone, including the Dahlan faction, especially since he has a role in negotiations, and his connections with Europe, the UAE, Egypt, and the United States, which cannot be ignored.”

But even with preparations underway for the elections, questions remain over both how much they will alter the existing balance of power, and whether they even will take place.

Al-Tanani stressed that Abbas continued to have leverage because of the power he holds.

“President Mahmoud Abbas in his electoral decrees and decisions has kept in his hands the authority of appointment for the [Palestinian] National Council membership, which means the ability to flip any majority that legislative elections might yield,” he observed in reference to the legislative body of the Palestinian Liberation Organisation (PLO), representing both Palestinians inside and outside the Palestinian territories.

That means that even if an opposition coalition is able to secure a majority, Abbas could potentially prevent them from holding power in the legislature and therefore in the PLO, which is the internationally-recognised representative of the Palestinian people.

And, al-Qarra pointed out, Abbas had another option – postponing the elections again, as he did in 2021 .

“If he feels that this [opposition] alliance is a real threat that he will lose, he will cancel the elections or postpone them, and the pretexts and justifications are many,” he said.

articles.title: Man spots wallaby hopping around English countryside
articles.summary: "You're not from around here, are you?" The post Man spots wallaby hopping around English countryside appeared first on Talker.
articles.body:
A wallaby has been spotted hopping around the Cornwall, England countryside.

Scot Weller was driving into Liskeard when he saw what he initially thought was a dog in the road ahead.

The owner of Original Cornish Pasties says the animal was jumping along the road in front of him as he drove to work.

No one knows how the marsupial native to Australia ended up in Cornwall.

Last month, a wallaby was also spotted in north Devon .

Scott said there were several cars behind him and, worried the animal could be hit, he decided to follow it.

The wallaby then made its way onto the sidewalk and stopped.

He said: "But then I realized it was hopping and that it was a wallaby on the loose."

Scott pulled alongside and said to the escaped marsupial: "Hello, you're not from around here, are you?"

The animal then disappeared down a side road toward the local Co-op.

"It was a bit sad that he was out there on his own, as there can't have been much for it to eat because of the heatwave we've been having ," Scott said.

"I just thought, 'Poor thing, he's lost.'"

He reported the sighting to police via 101, although the call handler initially had some trouble comprehending what he was reporting.

"I told her, 'There's a wallaby hopping up the street,' and she replied, 'The Australian animal, like a small kangaroo? Right, OK.'"

The wallaby has reportedly been sighted elsewhere in Liskeard.

A member of staff at the leisure center is also said to have spotted it at the weekend in the secondary school playing fields.

A Devon and Cornwall Police spokesperson said that the animal had disappeared by the time officers arrived.

They said: "We were called to a report of a wallaby seen on Dean Street, Liskeard, shortly before 6am today, August 24. Officers carried out an area search but did not locate the animal."

articles.title: France to ban ‘Black Friday’ in Franglais clampdown
articles.summary: France has restarted its long-running war on the English language with plans to ban the use of “Black Friday” and anglicised government slogans.
articles.body:
France has restarted its long-running war on the English language with plans to ban the use of "Black Friday" and anglicised government slogans.

The country's own culture ministry has cited the spread of "Black Friday" promotions in English as evidence that the 1994 Toubon law protecting the French language is ill-adapted to the internet age.

A new bill would require such foreign expressions in online advertising to carry French translations in equally large and prominent lettering.

The proposals have been lodged by Yan Chantrel, a Socialist senator. While their passage is not assured, they draw on a cross-party senate report backed by conservative and centrist colleagues.

Under the plans, multi-national companies could no longer address employees in France solely in English, while the proliferation of university courses taught entirely in English would be curbed.

Even state-backed slogans such as "Choose France" and "French Tech", which are dear to Emmanuel Macron , the French president, could be targets of the proposed clampdown, Mr Chantrel's office told The Telegraph.

Named after Jacques Toubon, Jacques Chirac's culture minister, the 1994 law was designed to guarantee a "right to French" in advertising, employment, education and public services. Yet the internet, globalisation and the spread of English have sorely tested its reach.

Few cases illustrate that better than "Let's Grau", the Franglais tourism slogan adopted by Le Grau-du-Roi, a Mediterranean resort, in 2015.

French-language campaigners fought a lengthy legal battle to have it banned, only for the Conseil d'État, France's highest administrative court, to rule in 2020 that the town could keep it because no officially approved French equivalent existed.

Nicolas Polge, the court's public rapporteur, called the slogan "unfortunate" and even mocked another southern tourism brand, "So Toulouse", wondering whether English speakers might hear "so to lose".

His legal conclusion was nevertheless categorical: the campaigners stood no chance without an overhaul of the Toubon law.

Mr Chantrel now wants to do precisely that. His office said the wording would be tightened so that a public authority should no longer be able to escape the law in the same way as Le Grau-du-Roi.

The bill would also address digital communications that fall outside legislation conceived in the internet's infancy.

Mr Chantrel wants the French translation of foreign wording in online advertising to have "equal legibility".

His office confirmed that would mean the same-size lettering, preventing advertisers from displaying an English slogan prominently while reducing its French equivalent to tiny print.

Public services and local authorities would face stricter obligations, while the government's official guardian of the French language, DGLFLF, would gain stronger powers to investigate and sanction breaches, inspired by Quebec's powerful language watchdog. The precise sanctions have yet to be set out.

The bill, lodged on Aug 12, follows a 2024 Senate inquiry co-written by Mr Chantrel with Catherine Belrhiti of the conservative Republicans and centrist Pierre-Antoine Levi, which called for the Toubon law to be "updated, strengthened and better applied".

It comes amid recurrent French alarm over the advance of "globish".

In 2022, the Académie Française, official guardians of the French language, threatened legal action over English words such as "surname" appearing on France's new identity cards.

Marine Le Pen, a nationalist French presidential candidate, also pledged to ban the use of foreign words in advertising and public communication as part of an "emergency plan" to "save" the French language.

A year later, Jean-Marie Rouart, one of the academy's "immortals", accused Mr Macron of being the "Tartuffe of the French language" for inaugurating a €2100m temple to French at Villers-Cotterêts while embracing slogans such as "One Planet Summit" and "Choose France".

He accused the president of participating in French's "slow destruction".

Language purists complained that the name Lorraine Airport infringed language laws with its use of English and was an insulting example of "Anglo-mania". It was told to change its name to Lorraine Aéroport.

Timed to coincide with Paris Fashion Week, purists also hoped to oust terms such as "must-have", "lifestyle" and "try before you buy".

articles.title: Worker jabbed with needle after Glasgow bin lorry fire
articles.summary: The fire happened on Oban Drive at about 11:30 and forced the refuse vehicle to dump its rubbish on the street.
articles.body:
A council worker has been jabbed with a needle while cleaning up rubbish following another bin lorry fire in Glasgow.

The fire happened in Wilton Court at about 11:30 and forced the refuse vehicle to dump its rubbish on the street. Discarded vapes were found among the waste.

GMB union convener Chris Mitchell said the worker was jabbed with the needle during the clean-up and was taken to hospital for a Hepatitis B injection as a precaution.

It is understood to be the ninth fire in a Glasgow bin lorry this year, with the council previously urging the public to recycle batteries and vapes properly.

The fire happened four hours into the refuse workers' shift.

Mitchell said: "The crew acted with professionalism and made sure the load was safely ejected on the street before causing further damage.

"The crew and the general public were not harmed."

He said he was awaiting details as to how the fire started but said it could have been "another lithium battery fire".

"We would like to thank the cleansing teams for cleaning the area up," he said.

"Unfortunately, during the cleaning process another accident occurred where a council worker was jagged by a hypodermic needle.

"I would encourage the wider public when disposing of lithium batteries or sharp items to dispose of them properly.

"I will make this clear: we are one fire away from serious harm or damage."

Two weeks ago a bin lorry caught fire in Glasgow's Jamaica Street , prompting the council to issue a warning over the dangers of throwing batteries in normal rubbish.

There was a similar fire involving a bin lorry in Edinburgh last month.

A spokesman for Glasgow City Council said: "Our staff raised the alarm of a fire within their vehicle this morning and followed the correct procedure by unloading the waste onto the street.

"A cause for the fire has still to be confirmed, but discarded vapes were found within the waste that was off-loaded.

"If a discarded vape is confirmed as the cause of the fire, this incident will again highlight the danger linked to disposing of batteries and vapes in general waste."

He said the quick response of the crew ensured they were unharmed and the risk of damage to the vehicle was minimised.

"But it is vital that we all take care to recycle batteries and vapes properly," he said.

"Batteries and vapes can be safely recycled at a wide range of shops or at any of our household waste recycling centres."

A spokesman for the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said it was alerted to the fire in a bin lorry on Wilton Court at 11:28 and sent two appliances to the scene.

He said one casualty was taken to hospital and crews left the scene at 13:04 after ensuring the area had been made safe.

articles.title: Beyond China's humanoid robots, a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
articles.summary: There are more than two million robots working in China's factories - and they are scaling up fast.
articles.body:
Watch: BBC visits factories in China with robot workers

"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.

His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."

A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".

For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.

The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.

Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.

It is a commitment that will surely change the world, much like the last time the Chinese economy underwent a massive transformation. It is already shipping its robots across the globe: more than half of the world's industrial robots are now made in China.

What is less clear is the impact of such sweeping automation in a country that sits at the heart of global manufacturing, trade and innovation. What does this mean for China's human workforce, for instance? And how would we be able to truly measure the cost of this transformation in a regime that controls information so tightly?

The future of China's workers is uncertain in the industrial revolution the world has been watching: gleaming solar grids, peak hours made noiseless by electric vehicles, machines that run faster than Usain Bolt. Over the weekend, China hosted the second edition of the World Humanoid Games where robots boxed, sprinted and marched.

What is fuelling this spectacle is another, less visible revolution happening inside factories and classrooms.

The BBC has visited industrial sites where we have been shown robots that do not look human, or dance or leap on stage but weld, paint, lift, assemble and work around the clock without a break or benefits. Some are designed to build more robots. We have also been inside academies where China is training the people who will work alongside its robotic workforce.

This is a front-row seat to what Xi calls China's "new productive forces" - and how they could reshape the country.

On a factory floor in the southern city of Chengdu, the old and and the new are working side by side.

An assembly line of around 30 middle-aged men and women is screwing, drilling and polishing CRP Technology's signature product: a robotic arm which performs various industrial tasks. Also in the room are four young engineers crowded around a console, trying to crack the code for a prototype, a new robot that they hope will help build other robots.

One of them, 31-year-old Pang Kai, who is part of the research and development team, pushes the sleek skeleton across the room. Because China's future workforce is not quite ready to strut out. For now, it can only do simple repetitive movements, such as scan a QR code.

"Maybe in another half year, it can do another task," Pang says, smiling wistfully. It's a long road and the team are celebrating every small win.

CRP Technology, which employs around 300 people, has been building robot arms for nine years. Each arm can be tailored to a factory's needs to help build cars, electronics or wind turbines. The firm says a single arm can be programmed to perform more than 90% of repetitive tasks.

The engineers also wonder if, one day, they can replace the company's workforce. "We want our new robot to be like human beings. We hope it can think by itself," says Pang. "We need these kinds of robots because maybe in 10 years, we won't have enough workers in China."

A shrinking population and an ageing workforce is another reason Beijing is in a hurry to revolutionise its factories. By 2035, more than a third of China's population will be over 60, according to official estimates. The country will also lose nearly 60 million people in the next decade - almost equivalent to the population of France - according to some estimates.

The hope is that increased automation will fill this looming gap in the workforce before it starts to affect an already sluggish economy. But the speed of the transition is key. Around 120 million people still work in the manufacturing sector. If China moves too quickly, job losses could follow dealing a catastrophic blow to millions who depend on factory wages.

"In theory, machines can work 24 hours a day, which is certainly an advantage compared with human workers. But machines also require maintenance. Every day we need time for that, and each month the production line also requires inspection and repair," says Cao Li, vice-president of EV maker Leapmotor.

Increasingly popular in Europe and the UK, the company's budget-friendly, tech-focused cars come together at the Hangzhou factory with robots aiding the process at every step. At the end of the assembly line, more humans emerge.

The company has more than 25,000 workers and hundreds of them make the final checks as the sparkling new vehicles roll past. Will there be a day when they are no longer needed?

"It's entirely possible," Cao says. "And it may come relatively quickly. In workshops, including stamping, welding, and painting, we've basically achieved 100% automation."

China has the edge over the US due to its enormous manufacturing base. Motors, batteries, electronics, gears, sensors - everything needed to build the body of a robot is all at hand.

"China also has an idea. It has a plan. They know where they want to be in five years. They plan at a top level, but they break it down to the regions, to the municipalities," says Dr Susanne Bieller, General Secretary of the International Federation of Robotics.

"If you want to build a robot in Shenzhen - there's an entire ecosystem. It takes you less than one hour to source the components you need to make a robot. In Europe it can take you up to a week."

However, she acknowledges that while China is good at building the body, the US is still leading at building the "brain", which includes developing the AI to programme robots. And yet Chinese firms, from DeepSeek to Moonshot, have been unveiling new AI models that they say can compete with top US firms.

Driven by an "open-source" approach, where AI start-ups share their code, Chinese innovation has been able to catch up faster than expected, despite US export controls over critical advanced chips. Analysts now believe that the next leg of this race will be determined not by who has the best language model, but who can put this intelligence into millions of machines.

And that is why China is also investing in producing a generation of students learning to imagine what could come next.

At the Hangzhou Technician Institute, for example, children can start from the age of 15. And the scale of what is being taught can feel staggering. There is an entire building dedicated to engines and aeronautics, and a restricted floor for students who will work to keep China at the forefront of processing rare earths - another crucial commodity in the battle with Washington.

Some see this as a solution to China's stubbornly high youth unemployment rate, with one in five struggling to find a job. "Our students are in demand and can even be pre-booked by companies. They don't need to worry about employment at all, and we hold competitions as part of their training," Chen, the young teacher, says.

"It's better to find your position within the technological wave. In the process of progress, structural changes are bound to occur, and these structural changes are exactly where students' future employment opportunities lie."

But China still faces serious economic challenges, from a property crisis that continues to drag on to huge local government debt and persistently low consumption.

It is unclear if and how the revolution Beijing is touting will fix these, and it is hard to gauge how those whose jobs are threatened feel about the change that is coming. Will robots create prosperity for them, or simply take many of their jobs?

"My students ask me what will happen in the future," Chen says. "I say I don't know. Technology is changing so fast. But we can't just stand still and sleep here. We have to move forward to see what we are capable of doing."

articles.summary: A video has emerged showing a U.S. military C-17A Globemaster III aircraft approaching for a landing at Moscow, Russia's Vnukovo airport on Wednesday.
articles.body: Video captured a U.S. military transport plane coming in for a landing Tuesday at Moscow's Vnukovo airport, in a flight that the Kremlin reportedly claimed it had no information about. Data from the website Flightradar24 showed that the Boeing C-17A Globemaster III left Joint Base Andrews in Maryland early Sunday afternoon on a flight to Riga, Latvia. The aircraft then traveled from Riga to Moscow, Russia on Wednesday morning. The last time a U.S.-registered jet made a direct flight to Russia from Europe was in January when special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, visited Moscow for a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin about the war in Ukraine, according to Reuters. A Department of War spokesperson told Fox News Digital on Tuesday, "We have nothing to provide on this subject." Fox News Digital also has reached out to the White House and the U.S. Embassy in Moscow for comment. articles.title: Israel takes control of UN training centre for Palestinians
articles.summary: Israeli forces took control of a vocational training centre run by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees in an east Jerusalem suburb on Tuesday, in its late...
articles.body:
Israeli forces took control of a vocational training centre run by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees in an east Jerusalem suburb on Tuesday, in its latest move targeting the beleaguered organisation.

The raid drew condemnation from UN chief Antonio Guterres, and followed warnings by UNRWA that Israeli authorities were threatening its Qalandia training centre, located between the east Jerusalem neighbourhood of Kafr Aqab and the Qalandia refugee camp.

The centre was established in 1952 and offers vocational training to around 340 Palestinians from the occupied West Bank every year, according to UNRWA.

"In accordance with my directive and following the law we passed, today the evacuation of the UNRWA compound in Kafr Aqab in Jerusalem has begun," a statement from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said.

"The State of Israel will not allow an organisation whose employees were involved in terrorism and in the October 7 massacre to operate within its territory and will act against it with all available means," it added.

Israel has repeatedly accused UNRWA of providing cover for Hamas militants, claiming that some of its employees took part in the group's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel that sparked the war in Gaza.

Legislation severing ties with the agency and banning it from operating on Israeli territory took effect in January 2025.

A series of investigations, including one led by France's former foreign minister Catherine Colonna, found some "neutrality-related issues" at UNRWA but stressed Israel had not provided conclusive evidence for its headline allegation.

Guterres's spokesman said the secretary-general was "greatly alarmed" by Tuesday's incursion, adding that the training centre "and other UNRWA premises are premises of the United Nations. They are inviolable and immune from any form of interference."

Israeli ambassador to the UN Danny Danon said his office had sent a letter to Guterres on Tuesday saying UNRWA had no property rights to the compound.

"In addition, Israel notified both the agency and the United Nations in advance of its obligation to cease operations in Jerusalem and vacate the premises," he said, adding the grounds would be converted into an educational and community centre.

UNRWA said that Israeli forces "forcibly entered" the training centre at around 10 am (0700 GMT), with at least four armoured vehicles entering the premises, accompanied by more than 50 Israeli security personnel.

Around 20 UNRWA staff were on site at the time, it said, "unequivocally" condemning the incursion.

The "entry of armed security forces into a United Nations facility, without the authorisation or consent of the United Nations, is unacceptable", it added.

Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, on Tuesday celebrated "making history".

"Large forces of the Israel police are operating together with the relevant bodies to implement the law and remove UNRWA from the site," he said on Telegram.

He later posted a photo of the Israeli flag hoisted above the entrance to the training centre with the caption: "UNRWA in our hands."

An AFP journalist at the scene on Tuesday said Israeli forces had closed the main road near the entrance to the training centre.

Israel occupied and annexed east Jerusalem in 1967, in a move not recognised by much of the international community.

Israel's foreign ministry on Tuesday announced that the Jerusalem municipality had begun work on a "new educational and community complex in Jerusalem's Kafr Aqab neighbourhood".

"Despite holding no property rights to the plot, UNRWA has walled off the land for decades," it said in a statement.

The raid on the Qalandia centre comes a day after representatives from more than 25 diplomatic missions and international organisations visited the site.

The Palestinian foreign ministry condemned Tuesday's actions by Israel, saying they sought "to challenge the status and immunities of the United Nations and to impose facts on the ground by force".

In January, Israel began demolitions at UNRWA's headquarters in east Jerusalem, in what the organisation called an "unprecedented attack".

articles.title: Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs on US as high as 50%
articles.summary: The latest escalation in an ongoing trade war between the US and Canada will see new levies on goods from steel to furniture, fresh tuna and makeup.
articles.body:
Canada has announced counter-tariffs as high as 50% on a range of US goods in retaliation to the latest wave of levies on Canadian imports imposed by President Donald Trump last weekend.

The Canadian tariffs will apply to nearly C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) worth of American products, ranging from steel to furniture, fresh tuna and cotton T-shirts, officials announced on Tuesday.

The list of targeted products is designed to match Canadian goods hit by the US. The Canadian levies are set to come into effect on 8 September.

It is the latest escalation after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making last-minute demands that were unreasonable.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said that Canada's retaliation is in response to 50% tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on a range of Canadian goods after trade talks fell apart on Friday.

"Those tariffs will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses and communities across our nation," he said. "Canada must respond."

Champagne characterised Canada's retaliation as "proportionate" and "strategic".

He added that Canada will also offer businesses and workers impacted by US tariffs an additional C$7.5bn for support programmes designed to minimise job losses and keep companies afloat.

Placing taxes on trade between what are historically two of the world's closest trading partners will undoubtedly lead to pain on both sides of the border.

Supply chains which have been developed over decades are set to see increased trading costs due the latest tariff announcements made from both the US and Canada, ultimately hitting businesses of all sizes and consumers through potentially higher prices.

Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support their government in holding firm against the US.

But some questions remain on exactly why trade talks fell apart, with the Conservative opposition asking that the full text of the draft deal with the US be released.

Businesses have also expressed concerns about the impact of a prolonged trade war with Canada's largest trading partner.

The White House released a statement after Canada announced its counter-tariffs, saying that the US was prepared to offer Canada "the most preferential market access of any country on Earth" in recent trade talks.

"Instead of partnership, Canada chose unreasonable demands, walk-backs, and flat-out rejection," it said.

In a series of Tuesday posts on Truth Social, Trump also accused Canada of "ripping off" the US for decades and of charging American farmers steep tariffs.

"I deal with many countries, and Canada is easily the most difficult and unreasonable," Trump wrote. "They feel entitled, but they are not a State, and will be entitled no longer!"

He suggested that he will change the name of Lake Ontario, one of the Great Lakes on the US-Canada border, to Lake America, writing: "We don't expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer."

Trump threatened this week to hike US tariffs on Canadian automobiles to 50% as of 1 January.

Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by accusing Trump of wanting to "destroy" Canadian industries including the automobile manufacturing and steel and aluminum sectors.

Public rhetoric on both sides reached a fever pitch on Monday, but some officials struck a more diplomatic tone on Tuesday with hopes that talks could be resumed.

After calling Trump a "loser" on Monday at a news conference, Ontario Premier Doug Ford acknowledged in an interview with CNN that "things got a little heated".

"But I want to make a deal — a good deal for the American people, a good deal for Canadians," Ford said.

The escalation also puts into question the future of a North American free trade pact between Canada, the US and Mexico called the USMCA.

President Claudia Sheinbaum had despatched her economy secretary, Marcelo Ebrard, to Washington for emergency talks after trade negotiations collapsed with Canada.

Canada released on Tuesday a list of nearly 900 US products that will be hit by its counter-tariffs.

A 50% tariff on steel and aluminum products that were previously only subject to a 25% counter tariff

A 50% tariff on various other goods including natural honey, furniture, clothing and apparel, makeup and perfume

A 25% tariff on goods including appliances, like dishwashers and washing machines, dairy products, such as cheese, fish and seafood, and certain steel and aluminum derivative products

A 15% tariff on certain types of tools and machinery, including forklifts and air conditioning machines

Canadian officials said they chose products that consumers and businesses in Canada could source elsewhere in an attempt to minimise hurt at home.

articles.title: Dangerous debris washes ashore before beachgoer makes another troubling find
articles.summary: A Jersey Shore beachgoer says she found more needle plungers and drug paraphernalia the day after Manasquan Beach reopened following a syringe cleanup.
articles.body: A popular Jersey Shore beach reopened to swimmers after dozens of syringes washed ashore — only for a beachgoer to report finding more concerning debris along the sand the following day. The syringes and paraphernalia were discovered littered across the sands of Manasquan Beach in Manasquan, New Jersey, along the Jersey Shore, on Saturday. Officials at the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) said the debris included household waste, including syringes used for at-home insulin injections, according to local outlets. DANGEROUS WATER WARNINGS HIT TRENDY VACATION SPOT AFTER POWERFUL STORM POUNDS AREA Mayor Michael Mangan told Fox News Digital the syringes were first discovered Saturday afternoon and were cleaned up and properly cleared away.  "There was a large amount of additional debris, indicating a garbage spill of some kind, and the incident was localized to the south end beach, along the Manasquan Inlet jetty," Mangan said. It's believed the debris washed ashore following recent heavy rainfall and sewer overflows, according to local reports citing the NJDEP. Mangan added that, in accordance with guidance from the NJDEP and Monmouth County health officials, the town waited for two high-tide cycles, which occurred overnight Saturday. SUMMER TRAVELERS WARNED AFTER FECAL BACTERIA LEVELS IN WATER EXCEED SAFETY STANDARDS By 9 a.m. Sunday, state and local officials "met on site, and no syringes were observed — so the water was reopened," Mangan told Fox News Digital. But not all residents agreed with the timing of reopening the waters. Priscilla Mahajan, a Manasquan resident, told local outlet News 12 she found needle plungers and drug paraphernalia on Sunday. Mahajan had participated in the cleanup efforts the day before. She said she felt the beach reopened too soon. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "One beach cleanup is definitely not enough to say something is safe," the resident said. Mahajan added, "We can't change what's in the ocean or what people have done in the past, but we can change our reaction to it." Mahajan told CBS News she found syringes, cut straws, syringe plungers, syringe caps and small plastic baggies along the beach. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Fox News Digital reached out to the NJDEP, but the agency declined to comment. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The syringe discovery comes less than two weeks after another unusual scene unfolded along the Jersey Shore, when nearly 30 dead juvenile dogfish sharks were found scattered across a beach in Sea Isle City. At the time, shark ecologist Mike Heithaus told Fox News Digital that seeing so many sharks wash ashore at one time was rare. articles.title: 'Country is not a dharamshala': Amit Shah sets target for illegal immigration-free India
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Home minister Amit Shah on Tuesday said the Narendra Modi govt has set a goal to make the country illegal immigration-free in a âvery short.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Home minister Amit Shah on Tuesday said the Narendra Modi govt has set a goal to make the country illegal immigration-free in a âvery short period of timeâ and, for this purpose, reached out to the border states over the past eight months, sharing with them its document on a quadrangular approach to border security.The policy drawn up by the Centre enlists the border guarding forces, state and district administration, relevant arms of govt of India and local citizens as key stakeholders in securing the borders.Addressing the valedictory session of the national security strategy conference (NSSC) organised by Intelligence Bureau here, Shah reiterated that âthis country is not a Dharamshala and only the citizens have the right to live hereâ. âInfiltrators are a threat of the countryâs security, economy and trigger unnatural demographic shifts,â he stated at the event attended by over 850 officials of the Central security agencies and forces, the state/UT police and intelligence agencies.With NSSC focused on anticipating security trends and challenges over the next 15-20 years and devising strategies to avert them, Shah underlined that challenges should be identified and destroyed before they become big. "By creating such an ecosystem, we will be able to create a secure, infiltrator-free and narcotics free India,â he told the officers that included both young ones at the cutting-edge level and their seasoned, experienced seniors.Stating that PM Narendra Modi had set the target of making the nation developed by 2047, Shah said the first condition for this would be making its internal security more robust.Commending the state police forces, central agencies and the Central armed police forces (CAPFs) for having eliminated the challenge posed by three hotspots â J&K, Left-wing extremism-hit areas and the north-east â the home minister said that had the past governments visualised these problems before they became acute, the country would not have had to bear the brunt of them for decades.Shah also described the dismantling of the Popular Front of India (PFI) network âin one nightâ (in multi-state raids of Sept 2022), apart from imposing a ban on it, as âan excellent instance of Centre-state coordinationâ.The home minister emphasised on the need to take the countryâs first anti-terror doctrine â PRAHAAR â from document to practice, to âeradicate terrorism and dismantle the terror ecosystemâ. He said the govt has strengthened the anti-fugitive drive, having deported 274 fugitives from different countries between 2019 and 2026. âAll the states should aim to bring the fugitives back to face the law here,â he stated.Stating that global instability, lack of energy security, supply chain disruption and increasing radicalisation of cyber misinformation have emerged as the key challenges, Shah insisted that the security policy taken each of these into account and aim to effectively tackle them.With the latest focus of the home minister being to eliminate the drugs menace, Shah sought the cooperation of the states in making the country narcotics-free."Police of all states should implement the Narcotics Control Vision Document 2026-2029 on the ground to protect the new generation and work on three D's âdetect, disrupt and destroyâ for "a drug-free India,â he stated.Shah also asked the officers to used the integrated data bank of CCTNS, ICJS, Natgrid and NAFIS to develop actionable intelligence through data integration, analysis and identification of modus operandi through AI, so that future challenges can be prevented.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Dolly Parton, country music icon, dies at 80
articles.summary: The “Queen of Country” won 11 Grammys and sold over 100 million records, making her one of the bestselling performers of all time.
articles.body: Dolly Parton, who rose from a loving if impoverished upbringing in the mountains of East Tennessee to become the “Queen of Country” music, a Hollywood star and a beloved American icon, has died, her family announced Tuesday. She was 80. Her team confirmed the death and said the star had faced a brief battle with cancer and died Tuesday surrounded by her loved ones. Parton’s nephew, Brian Seaver, announced the news in a video posted on her Instagram. “My name is Brian Seaver, son of Cassie Parton, and I’m representing the Parton and Owens family today announcing the passing of my aunt, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, Sister, Sis and Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next,” Seaver said in a video. “This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it till now,” he added. Seaver added that Parton “lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by [her late husband] Carl, her parents, and countless others.” “Rest in peace, Aunt Dolly — Aunt, Granny, Gigi. May God bless Dolly Parton, and may God bless you all. She will always love you,” Seaver said at the end of the video statement. The star’s team honored her legacy, saying she “spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched.” “Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand,” Team Dolly said in a statement Tuesday. “Dolly’s unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact.” As word of Parton’s death spread, the tributes began pouring in. President Donald Trump ordered U.S. flags lowered to half-staff nationwide for one week while a constellation of the entertainment world’s biggest stars weighed in with condolences. Her death comes after Parton announced in May that she was canceling a Las Vegas show and had been undergoing treatment for kidney stones for several years. "Lord, they dig more stones out of me a year than the rock quarry in Rockwood, Tennessee," Parton said in a statement. "But seriously, my immune system and my digestive system got all out of whack over the past couple three years, and they’re working real hard on rebuilding and strengthening those, and hopefully, I’ll be up to snuff again soon." On Friday, Parton acknowledged she had lost a step after her husband, Carl Dean, died in March 2025. But she insisted she wasn’t ready to leave the stage. “Even though I’m still healin’,” Parton told People. “I’m still workin’! You know me — as I’ve often said — I’ve dreamed myself into a corner, and I still have so many things I want to achieve, so I’m gonna keep on working as long as I can to see everything come to life.” During her more than 60-year career, Parton sold over 100 million records and won 11 Grammy Awards, making her one of the bestselling musical performers of all time. Parton also became a star on the silver screen, gaining a whole new audience and critical acclaim when she brought her Southern charm to movies like “9 to 5” (she wrote and sang the theme song), “Steel Magnolias” and "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas." Bedecked in blond bouffant hairdos and never without her makeup, Parton also became one of the nation’s best-known brands who parried questions about her hourglass figure and augmented breasts with her signature self-deprecating wit. “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap,” Parton once said. Parton was a shrewd businesswoman who amassed an estimated $650 million fortune and maintained creative control in the cutthroat and male-dominated music industry. She presided over an entertainment empire that included the Dollywood theme park. And she was a devoted philanthropist who launched the Dollywood Foundation to provide poverty relief and fund educational programs in her native East Tennessee. Never shy at expressing her Christian faith, Parton was also a public supporter of the LGBTQ community who advocated for marriage equality and spoke up in defense of transgender people. “I keep saying: If you’re the fine Christian that you think you are, why are you judging people,” Parton said during a 2017 interview with Larry King. “That’s God’s job.” Along those lines, she jokingly told a British outlet a few years earlier: “I think gay couples should be allowed to marry. They should suffer just like us heterosexuals.” Through it all Parton leaned on the love of her life, her husband Carl, who died at 82 and who, from the moment they married in 1966, happily ceded the spotlight to his world-famous wife. “Words can’t do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years,” Parton said in July 2025. Born Jan. 19, 1946, in a one-room cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River near the town of Sevierville, Parton was the fourth of 12 children. Her father, Robert Lee Parton, could not read or write and often supplemented the family's meager income from their farm by working construction jobs. Her mother, Avie Lee Parton, ran the household and was fond of singing traditional Appalachian ballads. The future superstar said it was her mother who instilled in her a love for music. And it was at church that Parton started performing. By age 13, she was singing on local radio and television shows and made her debut at the Grand Ole Opry, where she met Johnny Cash. “Dolly Parton has one of the most distinctive voices in American pop music,” Katherine Dacey, a professor at the Berklee College of Music, told NBC News before Parton’s death. “Her high soprano voice gets its distinctive character from her fast vibrato and vocal twang.” The day after she graduated from Sevier County High School in 1964, Parton headed to Nashville, where she first made her mark writing songs for other performers, some of them with her uncle Bill Owens. In songs like “Tennessee Homesick Blues” and “Coat of Many Colors,” Parton drew inspiration from her hardscrabble childhood. Three years after leaving school, Parton released her first record, “Hello, I'm Dolly,” and caught the attention of country star Porter Wagoner and became a regular on his shows. Then, in 1974, Parton broke out on her own when she topped the country charts for the first time with a song she wrote and performed called “Jolene.” She later revealed it was inspired by a bank teller who flirted with her husband when they were newlyweds. Her next four singles were also country chart-toppers, and one of them, “I Will Always Love You,” later became a huge hit for Whitney Houston in 1992. Parton also won her first Grammy with a single from that record called “Here You Come Again.” Parton, who earned a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1984, made several more movies and performed around the world, but she always returned to the music that first made her famous — and to the hollers of East Tennessee where she was born and where she and her husband made their home. “Never ignore your roots — your home or your hair,” she once said. In 1986, Parton opened the Dollywood theme park in the Great Smoky Mountains near her hometown. The 165 acres include roller coasters, a bald eagle sanctuary and music and crafts that pay tribute to the region's Appalachian heritage. Parton and her husband never had children. And in public statements, Parton said she “believed that God didn’t mean for me to have kids.” “Since I had no kids, and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom,” Parton told Oprah Winfrey in 2020. “So I think a big part of my whole success is the fact that I was free to work.” Parton also left her fans guessing about her politics, although in 2016 she angered many Republicans by saying that Hillary Clinton was “very qualified” to be president. In an online post, Parton insisted she was not endorsing Clinton or Clinton's then-rival, Donald Trump. “I try not to get political but if I am, I might as well just run myself ‘cause I’ve got the hair for it, it’s huge, and they could always use more boobs in the race,” she wrote. While she generally dodged commenting on partisan politics, Parton was hailed in 2020 for helping to fund research at Vanderbilt University that led to the development of Moderna's Covid vaccine. “My longtime friend Dr. Naji Abumrad, who’s been involved in research at Vanderbilt for many years, informed me that they were making some exciting advancements towards research of the coronavirus for a cure,” Parton tweeted in April 2020, as much of the nation was under lockdown. She added that she would be donating $1 million to the research. Abumrad, who treated Parton when she was in a car accident in 2013, became friends with the country star afterward. “Without a doubt in my mind, her funding made the research toward the vaccine go 10 times faster than it would be without it,” he told The Washington Post in November 2020. Parton's philanthropic legacy also includes the creation of the Imagination Library, which mails free books to children around the world. In the three decades since it was founded, the organization has mailed more than 300 million books to kids around the U.S., as well as Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland. The initiative was inspired by Parton’s father, who was illiterate. Parton often spoke about his intelligence and strength of character but said she believed his inability to read and write held him back. “When I got this idea to do the Imagination Library, I wanted to get Daddy involved in it. I wanted him to help me with that so he could take the pride in that and so he did,” she wrote on her website in 2020. “He got to live long enough to hear the kids call me the Book Lady.”

articles.body:
The United States’ spy chief is reportedly visiting Moscow for meetings, according to US media outlets, even as the Kremlin says no talks with US envoys are planned this week.

CBS News, citing unnamed sources familiar with the situation, reported that CIA Director John Ratcliffe was in the Russian capital on Tuesday.

The outlets did not say whom he was meeting or what the talks are expected to cover. The CIA declined to comment, according to the Reuters news agency.

The news comes after a US military transport aircraft travelled from Riga to Moscow, according to flight-tracking websites.

Russia, meanwhile, said no talks between Moscow and US envoys are planned this week, as Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations remain stalled.

“No, there are no such plans,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a press briefing on Tuesday.

Asked about reports that a US military plane landed in Moscow on Tuesday morning, Peskov said he had “no such information”.

Later, the ⁠plane ⁠believed to be carrying Ratcliffe departed Moscow, according to data on the flight-tracking website.

Ratcliffe’s reported visit comes as US-brokered talks aimed at ending Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have stalled. But Moscow earlier this month freed a former US Marine detained since 2022 amid concerns about his health.

Axios also reported that Washington informed Ukraine of a senior delegation traveling to Moscow in advance and asked it to suspend strikes until it leaves, quoting a source with knowledge of the matter.

The Iran war is also a live issue between Washington and Tehran’s ally, Moscow.

CIA Director Ratcliffe has been reportedly central to high-profile prisoner exchanges between the US and Russia since US President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, including the release of a US-Russian dual national, Ksenia Karelina.

If confirmed, the reports of his visit would mark the first such trip since then-CIA Director William Burns travelled to Moscow in 2021.

articles.title: Iran and Oman negotiate joint Strait of Hormuz shipping corridor
articles.summary: The two countries are also discussing a joint mine-clearing mission, even as President Trump said the U.S. Navy had already removed all mines from the waterw...
articles.body:
Iran and Oman met on Tuesday to negotiate a temporary joint shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, along with a mission to clear mines from the critical oil export route.

Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr bin Hamad Albusaidi called his meeting with Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi in Tehran productive, expressing optimism that a temporary corridor and "practical arrangements to restore safe navigation" would be unveiled in short order. Oman's Foreign Ministry posted on social media that the framework under discussion envisions a joint mine-clearing effort, with both nations committed to further talks aimed at establishing a lasting corridor and governance structure for the strait.

The diplomats did not reach a deal, according to Axios . In a joint statement, Iran and Oman said they are also discussing a mechanism for information exchange, traffic management, and maritime and security services.

The talks came on the same day President Donald Trump announced that the U.S. Navy had completed its own mine-removal operation. "I have just been informed by the United States Navy that all mines have been removed and/or detonated from within the International Waters of the Strait of Hormuz," Trump wrote on Truth Social. He warned that Iran has been put on notice that any vessel caught laying new mines would be "immediately and systematically destroyed," and he noted that the U.S. Space Force has the waterway under surveillance.

Oman's reference to a mine-clearing mission appeared to contradict Trump's statement, according to CNBC . Axios reported that two U.S. officials with direct knowledge of the operation corroborated Trump's claim, adding that the Navy spent several months deploying underwater drones to scan the Traffic Separation Scheme — the median lane of the strait — and identified more than 100 objects believed to be mines, which private contractors were then hired to remove or destroy.

The Iran-Oman discussions come against a backdrop of U.S. military escorts enabling tankers to move more than 660 million barrels of crude through the strait since early May , though throughput remains well below the roughly 20 million barrels per day the waterway handled before the conflict. Traffic has been routed through a southern lane hugging the Omani coastline, with U.S. officials telling Axios that the channel handled over 500 ship transits in the preceding month.

The Iran-Oman talks followed by one day Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's warning that the U.S. would impose sanctions on any nation conducting business with Iran, according to CNBC. Trump earlier this month threatened to bomb Oman if it "gets in the way."
