articles.title: Why Trump is escalating his trade war with Canada — and what it means for you
articles.summary: Both sides have announced new 50% tariffs that could make everyday goods more expensive. Trump has also threatened to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lak...
articles.body:
Canada on Tuesday announced new retaliatory tariffs as high as 50% on more than 700 U.S. goods, including steel, clothing, appliances, tools and fish. The new measures, which go into effect on Sept. 8, come after trade talks between the two countries collapsed over the weekend, sparking a full-blown trade war.

On Monday, two days after following through on an earlier tariff threat, President Trump threatened to increase tariffs on all cars, trucks, car parts and steel from Canada to 50% starting next year. Trump also said he's " giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America ."

Trump wrote Sunday on Truth Social that Canada was "among the worst Nations in the World to deal" with and warned that America's northern neighbor " will be treated like a State no longer ."

"The U.S.A. will always be far bigger, richer, and stronger than Canada," the president said in a subsequent post . "Someone should get these clowns to 'fall in line' or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!"

Trump's remarks — and Canada's response — followed weeks of negotiations and frequent claims from Trump that a deal was close. Both sides announced late Friday that they had failed to come to terms. At midnight on Saturday, the Trump administration followed through on its earlier threat to impose new 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods, including hockey sticks, plywood, men's suits, wine, cement, honey, makeup, perfume, jewelry, furniture and cameras.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney declared on Saturday that Canada was now "at war" with the U.S. over the tariffs, vowing a "dollar for dollar" response.

"We learned from the U.S. team during negotiations that [Trump] wants to destroy our major industries," Carney told reporters on Monday. "That's one of the major reasons that led us to say 'no.' It was a bad deal."

Can U.S.-Canada relations be repaired? If not, how will all of these new tariffs affect you? Trump has been trying to transform America's alliance with one of its biggest trading partners since returning to office in January 2025. Here's where things stand right now — and what could come next.

The U.S. and Canada have been conducting on-again, off-again trade talks since the start of Trump's second term. The latest round began in late July after Trump threatened to impose new 50% import taxes in response to Canada's retaliatory measures against his earlier waves of tariffs. The goal was to deescalate the dispute and reach some sort of lasting deal.

As recently as last week , leaders from both countries were saying that a deal was effectively done. The full details of the proposed agreement were never released, but the broad framework would have included Trump dropping his threat to impose the new 50% tariffs in exchange for removing what the U.S. views as unfair barriers to trade — particularly when it comes to agriculture and energy.

Another topic that was discussed was the revival of Keystone XL, a pipeline that was intended to carry large amounts of Canadian oil into the United States before the project was shuttered by former President Joe Biden. On Aug. 18, Trump posted on Truth Social that the U.S. and Canada had reached a deal and suggested that the pipeline could be "awoken from the grave."

The deal fell apart, however, after Canadian leaders said that the U.S. was trying to assert more control over their country's economy than it was willing to surrender.

"Last minute changes in the U.S. proposed deal were unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal," Carney wrote in a social media post Friday night in which he announced that he was formally suspending trade talks.

One of the big sticking points , Carney said, was American demands that amounted to "threats on the French language," which he said would "never be acceptable" in Canada's bilingual economy. Trump denied that language issues were ever part of the trade talks, saying, "This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister."

The breakdown of negotiations has sparked a renewed wave of threats and insults that appeared to be pushing the two countries even further apart.

Carney said Monday that Canada won't be returning to the negotiating table until he's confident the U.S. will approach any new talks with "the right attitude" and won't treat his country as a "subsidiary of the United States."

Doug Ford, the premier of the Canadian province of Ontario, was much less diplomatic. Standing in front of a sign that read "Protect Ontario" and flanked by construction workers on Monday, Ford urged Canada to inflict "massive pain" on the U.S. in retaliation for Trump's tariffs. He also took personal shots at the president, calling him a "loser" and telling Trump to "kiss my ass."

"He underestimates Canada. We're all in," Ford told the Associated Press . "Up here, we're at a fever pitch, everyone's in for an economic war."

Trump attacked Ford in kind in a post on Truth Social Monday, calling him a "flunky" and describing him as a "less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive" alternative to his late brother Rob Ford — who was mayor of Toronto from 2010 to 2014.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday suggested Canada was refusing to " negotiate in good faith " throughout the trade talks. He also suggested that Carney's choice to take a firm stance in trade talks was rooted more in his own political interests than the economic interests of the Canadian people.

"Unfortunately, Prime Minister Carney rose to power on an anti-American, anti-Trump platform. … He seems to have gone back to his old playbook," Bessent said.

Bessent's Canadian counterpart, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, told reporters Monday that his country can only tolerate so much from the U.S. before it is forced to punch back.

"At some stage you have to say enough is enough," he said. "We stood up for our economic sovereignty. … We're gonna be the master of our own destiny."

How the U.S.-Canada trade war could affect you

On Monday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that "there's no possible way" new tariffs "can really affect U.S. well-being."

But economists note that a tariff is an import tax paid by the company doing the importing — not by the foreign country (or foreign business) sending its goods to the U.S. The same experts have found that importers often pass at least some of the added cost of tariffs on to U.S. consumers through higher prices, rather than replacing the affected goods with American-made alternatives.

So it stands to reason that Trump's new 50% tariff on certain Canadian goods — hockey sticks, plywood, men's suits and so on — could make those products more expensive for Americans.

At the same time, U.S. businesses can suffer if they have to pay more for imported Canadian parts or raw materials, or if their products suddenly cost more in Canada because of retaliatory tariffs. Already, U.S. automakers have cut back production north of the border because of tariffs on steel and auto parts, which also raise repair and insurance costs. Meanwhile, Trump has complained that Canadian imports of American alcohol and cars have plummeted since last spring.

Canada's new retaliatory tariffs could have a similar effect on U.S. steel, clothing, fish, tools, appliances and other affected items.

On Monday, Ford also threatened to cut off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario. The Pentagon increasingly relies on the latter for use in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics. (For geopolitical reasons, it is always seeking sources other than China.) As for electricity, Ontario imposed a 25% surcharge on power exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York during an earlier phase of the U.S.-Canada dispute — then retreated when Trump threatened to double steel and aluminum tariffs.

But this time around, Ford insisted that "everything's on the table."

"We power 1.5 million [U.S.] homes and businesses," he said. "I'll do whatever it takes."

For the last 150 years , U.S. presidents have largely maintained close, cordial relations with America's " nicer " neighbors to the north. Trump, in contrast, spent the first weeks of his second term threatening to turn Canada into "the 51st state " and publicly referring to the country's then-prime minister and Liberal Party leader, Justin Trudeau, as "Governor" Trudeau .

In February 2025, Trump imposed sweeping 25% tariffs on goods from both Canada and Mexico. He later increased the tariff on many Canadian exports to 35% while imposing individual tariffs on steel, auto parts and other major industries.

Some have speculated that Trump's animosity toward Canada is rooted in his troubled business dealings there, including a Toronto hotel and condominium complex that went into receivership in 2016 and a Vancouver hotel that filed for bankruptcy and closed in 2020 . Others have noted Trump's fractious relationship with the progressive Trudeau, 54, who was famously photographed greeting first lady Melania Trump with a European cheek kiss at a 2019 Group of 7 gathering in France. A few months later, Trump called his Canadian counterpart "two-faced " for appearing to mock him at a meeting of NATO leaders. The previous year, Trump accused Trudeau of being "very dishonest and weak."

But the simpler explanation for Trump's aggressive trade stance is that the president might see Canada less as the United States' closest ally and more as yet another country that, in his view, has been freeloading and ripping America off — and he's determined to leverage Washington's vast economic power over Ottawa to renegotiate any existing deals on more favorable "America First" terms.

"It's not fair for us to be supporting Canada," Trump said at a Cabinet meeting in February 2025 . "If we don't support them, they don't subsist as a nation."

This is not a new theme for Trump. During his first term, he railed against the steep tariffs Canada imposes on U.S. dairy imports to protect its own domestic farmers, calling them a " disgrace ." In 2018, he slapped 25% tariffs on Canadian steel and 10% tariffs on Canadian aluminum — a move that resulted in at least 75,000 job losses across the U.S. manufacturing sector by mid-2019, according to economists .

Likewise, Trump has long complained that the modest U.S. trade deficit with Canada amounts to a "subsidy," even though experts say it mostly exists because the U.S. imports a lot of inexpensive Canadian oil, which helps lower Americans' gas prices . And Trump also disapproved of Canada spending less than 2% of its GDP on defense — a gripe he had with European NATO member nations as well. (Canada and others have since stepped up their spending .)

As a result, Trump has spent much of his second term escalating the economic pressure on Canada — imposing tariffs; stacking those tariffs with additional duties on steel and aluminum ; picking a trade fight over Canadian lumber ; withdrawing from earlier trade talks over a "fake" Ronald Reagan ad — in an apparent effort to use the United States' economic leverage over Canada to secure more favorable terms at the negotiating table.

Now, that campaign seems to have ruptured U.S.-Canada relations. Canadian sentiment toward the U.S. soured as soon as Trump started his "51st state" insults, according to the New York Times , with some Canadians boycotting American goods and canceling their U.S. vacations . The Canadian government imposed retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars of American exports; some provinces went so far as to pull certain U.S. products from their shelves. Trudeau's Liberal Party, which had been suffering in the polls, rebounded ahead of Carney taking over as prime minister in March and won last April's federal election. Since then, Carney has repeatedly said that Canada's old relationship with America is over.

articles.title: Penny Doe identified 36 years after remains found in Pennsylvania | Dateline
articles.summary: The remains were found in July 1990 in Monroe Township in Clarion County. Investigators are working to figure out what happened that summer.
articles.body: In July 1990, an unidentified woman was found in Clarion County, Pennsylvania. There was a penny in each of the woman’s jeans pockets, a small detail that would earn the woman a nickname: “Penny Doe.” For the past 36 years, her identity has remained unknown. Now, she has her name back. On Monday, Clarion County District Attorney Drew Welsh held a news conference to share the news. “Today is an important and significant day in the investigation into the death of Penny Doe,” he said. “Through the dedicated work of investigators over the past 36 years, today, I am able to reveal the identity of Penny Doe.” The DA outlined the steps taken over the last three decades of investigation. He described it as a “true team effort,” but cautioned that since the investigation is ongoing, some information would not be shared to protect the integrity of the case. “On July 22, 1990, a woman’s body was discovered in Monroe Township, Clarion County, by four local children,” Welsh recapped. “Three of those local children are here with us today.” In 2022, Dateline featured Penny Doe’s case in its “Cold Case Spotlight” digital series. We spoke with Angie Clinger, one of the children who found Penny Doe’s remains in a tunnel underneath a railroad trestle. “We freaked out,” she told Dateline in 2022. “I don’t think I ever ran so quick in my life.” The children reported their finding to the authorities, and the investigation began. The autopsy determined the unknown woman died as a result of “blunt trauma to the right side of her head,” Welsh said. “From that point forward, the death has been considered a homicide, and has remained open.” For the past 36 years, investigators have worked with two goals in mind. “The first was to identify who Penny Doe was, and the second was to prove what had happened to her and bring those responsible to justice.” Authorities have used various methods to try to identify her: fingerprint identification, checking her DNA against known missing persons, and testing her remains by analyzing her bones and teeth. “The Pennsylvania State Police have investigated and ruled out over 100 individuals of being Penny Doe,” Welsh stated. “There have been re-creations made of her face, and artists renderings of what she might have looked like.” A clay representation, illustrations and computer-generated images have also been made. And while those brought in leads and tips that were followed up on, they ultimately did not bring investigators any closer to finding her identity. Welsh said that from 1990 through 2020, when he began reviewing the case files, “there had been constant work done” by the Pennsylvania State Police. “After seeing all the hard work that came before me, I wanted to make sure that we got the case moving forward,” he said. They again looked into testing the DNA as technology continued to evolve. In 2023, police identified a funding source via a federal grant called the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant. In March 2024, they partnered with Othram Labs for a DNA extraction. A family tree was developed, and a potential sister identified. Police contacted the woman, who submitted her DNA, and the DNA came back as a match. “Ladies and gentlemen, Penny Doe has a name,” Welsh announced on Monday. “Penny Doe is Windy Buchanan.” She was born in October 1970 in Kentucky. Windy and her siblings did not have an easy upbringing, Welsh shared at the news conference. “The last time her family saw Windy, was that she and her family and two brothers pulled off on a random off-ramp looking for a place to rest and eat,” he said. “Windy’s last words to her family were, ‘Bye, Dad, I’m leaving.’” They never saw her again. Welsh would not share any additional information about where exactly that highway off-ramp was located. It is unclear where the off-ramp was in relation to the tunnel where the remains were found. Welsh said Windy’s family had searched for her over the years but were unsuccessful. Her younger sister, Tania Buchanan Boyd, spoke at the news conference, and shared more about who Windy was as a person. “My sister was fierce and she was kind, and she was loving,” she said. “She was the firstborn of five, and she would often watch over us.” “She was basically always there for me,” Tania said. “She was creative and artistic. She loved horses and animals. She was convinced that horseshoes brought good luck.” They weren’t the only things Windy believed brought good luck. “She always thought that finding a penny heads up brought you good luck,” Tania said. “Find a penny, pick it up. And all the day, you have good luck.” Tania also thanked the investigators who worked the case for more than three decades. “Our family deeply, deeply appreciates each and every one of you for staying with the case,” she said. “For many years we did search for Windy. We prayed that she would somehow be found, or that she might return to us one day.” “One of our deepest and longest-held prayers has finally been answered,” Tania said. “But it’s not over. We know where she was at, but we don’t know what happened to her.” “It’s important that our first goal has been accomplished,” Welsh stated. “My sincerest hope today is that this will start a new beginning to this investigation, where we will be able to answer that second question — that second goal — to find out who did this and bring them to justice.” Welsh urges anyone who knows anything about what happened to Windy Buchanan to please come forward. “It was easy for you to stay silent when it was an anonymous Penny Doe. Those days are done,” he said. “Now, you must speak.” “It’s never too late to come forward,” sister Tania said. “Windy deserves the truth, and our family deserves all of the answers.” If you have any information that could help the investigation, please contact the Pennsylvania State Police at 814-226-1710. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: Trump administration to revoke visas of short-term visitors seeking asylum
articles.summary: The state department says the number of revocations "remains dynamic" and would be carried out on a rolling basis.
articles.body:
The Trump administration plans to revoke the visas of foreign nationals who entered the US as short-term visitors and later applied for asylum.

"Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud - which is grounds for visa revocation," US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said.

Pigott said the number of revocations "remains dynamic" and would be carried out on a rolling basis. US media reports suggest hundreds of thousands of visas could be affected.

Since President Donald Trump took office, his administration has revoked more than 175,000 visas held by foreign nationals on various grounds, according to the State Department.

"Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio's leadership, we are making clear that a visa is a privilege — not a right," Pigott said in a statement to the BBC.

He said that the department is coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security to identify and revoke nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then filed for asylum to stay permanently.

"These types of visas are issued with the clear understanding that they are for those who intend to return home," he said.

Those who apply for those so-called short-term B1 and B2 visas are asked to pledge that they will not apply for asylum in the US.

Holders of B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026, who have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, will be revoked, the Associated Press reported, citing State Department documents.

The majority of business and tourism visas in 2024 were issued to citizens from Brazil, which obtained more than 1.1m B1 and B2 visas, mainland China, India and Pakistan, according to State Department data.

Just over 32,300 were issued to visitors from Great Britain and Northern Ireland in 2024.

Earlier this month, the state department said it had revoked more than 175,000 visas from foreign nationals who it said "violated the terms of their visas, committed crimes, called for violence against US citizens, defrauded Americans, abused our immigration system, or endangered national security".

The state department recently told embassies and consulates to reschedule visa interviews so that consular officers can complete training on a more restrictive policy.

The visa revocations come after a US judge last week struck down Trump's visa ban covering 75 countries, ruling that the policy - introduced when Trump returned to office in January 2025 - exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio's statutory authority.

In June, another US judge ruled against the administration's efforts to halt the processing of immigration applications from 39 countries.

articles.title: Syria ‘shakes off’ past with removal from US ‘terror’ list, says al-Sharaa
articles.summary: Removal of decades-old designation offers major sanctions relief for Syria, aiming to boost post-war reconstruction.
articles.body:
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa hailed the United States’ removal of his country from the “state sponsors of terrorism” list, a major sanctions relief step for a country aiming to boost post-war reconstruction.

“Today, Syria shakes off a dark stain and tears away a painful chapter of its past to embark on a path of development, reconstruction and rebuilding,” al-Sharaa said in a speech.

list 2 of 4 Syria, Israel hold US-mediated talks in Jordan to de-escalate tensions

list 3 of 4 ‘Barrel bomb mufti’ sentenced to life in Syria

list 4 of 4 US removes Syria from ‘state sponsor of terrorism’ list

Washington’s decision on Monday rescinded a decades-old designation that came with severe economic restrictions, marking another step in warming ties between the countries following the 2024 ouster of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad.

Al-Sharaa expressed his “many thanks to the President of the United States of America, Donald Trump, and to all the friendly and supportive nations that stood by us”.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement that Monday’s move “will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability”.

But the Treasury stressed that its removal of restrictions on Syria “does not change Treasury’s posture with regards to countering global terrorism and our commitment to hold bad actors in Syria accountable”.

The US listed Syria as a “state sponsor of terrorism” in 1979, accusing the country, then under the rule of Hafez al-Assad, Bashar’s father, of supporting Palestinian fighter groups and other armed movements in neighbouring Lebanon.

Monday’s move gave Syria “a path to prosperity”, according to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The action “eliminates the final major barriers for private sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy,” he said in a statement.

The World Bank estimates post-war reconstruction to cost more than $216bn.

Several countries welcomed the US move. Turkiye, a key backer of Syria’s new authorities, said the decision will “lend momentum to efforts to strengthen Syria’s ties with the international community and to establish lasting security and stability in the country”.

“At this stage, we call on the international community to unite its efforts toward the goal of a prosperous Syria and to fulfill its responsibilities to bring an end to aggressive actions that jeopardize this vision,” Ankara said.

Qatar and Jordan also welcomed the US decision, saying the move would support stability and recovery efforts in the country.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement that the step “supports the path of a political settlement in line with international legitimacy resolutions and the aspirations of the Syrian people”.

Jordan’s Foreign Ministry also welcomed the US decision, calling it “an important step” towards supporting Syria’s reconstruction, recovery and development.

Welcoming the move, Saudi Arabia wished Syria “further security, stability, and prosperity, and continued progress in its reconstruction and development efforts” in a way that would benefit the “aspirations of its people”.

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X that Ukraine had consistently supported Syria’s new government and people since the ouster of the Assad regime in their efforts to achieve recovery, peace and development.

In another sign of Syria’s growing international reintegration, Damascus also moved to expand its diplomatic outreach on Monday by launching an English-language social media account for its foreign media department.

Syrian Airlines will also begin operating regular direct flights from Damascus to Denmark’s capital, Copenhagen, and Austria’s capital, Vienna, on September 21, Syria’s civil aviation authority announced.

Omar al-Hosary, head of Syria’s General Authority of Civil Aviation and Air Transport, told the SANA news agency that the new routes are part of continuing efforts to expand the national carrier’s international network and strengthen air links between Syria and Europe.

articles.title: Dolly Parton obituary: The country legend who sang from the heart
articles.summary: The singer, songwriter and actress is known for timeless hits including Jolene and I Will Always Love You.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, the country singer from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, will be remembered for her songs that told beautiful stories so honestly, such as Coat of Many Colors, Jolene and I Will Always Love You.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy.”

She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her showbusiness career that spanned more than 60 years.

Dolly Rebecca Parton was born in 1946, the fourth of 12 children, into a poor farming family who lived in a one-bedroom cabin in Tennessee.

Her father, Robert Lee Parton, was a tobacco farmer and paid a missionary a sack of cornmeal for delivering her.

There was already music in the family - her mother, Avie Lee, sang folk songs all the time and her aunt played the guitar and wrote songs.

During some of Parton's earliest performances, her uncle, Bill Owens, accompanied her on the guitar - formative years for the future music legend.

From the age of six, she sang in the local church where her grandfather was the pastor, and was performing on her local TV station by the time she was a teenager.

In 1959, when she was 13 years old, Parton performed with Uncle Bill at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville - a live broadcast that is regarded as country music's biggest stage.

She was introduced by Johnny Cash and received three encores.

During her teenage years, Parton began to model herself on a local character who was known as the “town tramp”.

The lady wore bright red nail polish, low-cut tops and high heels - young Dolly thought she was beautiful.

When people said to her: “She ain’t nothing but trash”, Parton would reply: "Well, that’s what I’m gonna be when I grow up”.

Parton sang “ I’m just a backwards Barbie / too much make-up, too much hair ”, but her image was both a coat of armour and an astute disguise that helped get her noticed in showbusiness.

She would get ahead of the jokes by making them first, and had a quick and simple response for anyone who suggested she should tone it down: "Go to hell."

After graduating from high school in 1964, she moved to Nashville to launch her singing career and met her future husband, Carl Dean, on her very first day.

They married two years later and remained together until his death in 2025.

In Nashville, Parton's singing caught the eye of country performer Porter Wagoner, who hired her to perform on his television programme.

Over the next seven years, the pair became one of country music's most popular duos, releasing so many duets that many fans assumed they were a couple.

But their relationship was a complicated one, and as Parton's solo career started to rise, so did tensions behind the scenes.

Writing in her book Star of the Show: My Life on Stage, Parton said Wagoner saw her success away from his show as a "threat".

While travelling with Wagoner on a tour bus in 1969, Parton wrote Coat of Many Colors, a beautifully emotive tale of how she grew up poor, but rich with love.

Scrawled on the back of one of Wagoner's dry cleaning receipts, it was rated by Rolling Stone magazine as her second best-ever song. Years later, Parton named her own children's book Coat of Many Colors, and it was the name of a 2015 TV movie based on her life.

"It's a song that's just stood by me... it's created a life of many colours for me," she said.

Despite being unable to read sheet music, Parton played several instruments including the banjo, harp, piano and saxophone.

She had her first number one hit - and first Grammy nomination - with the song Joshua in 1971 and finally left The Porter Wagoner Show in 1974 to concentrate on her solo career.

To say goodbye to him, she wrote I Will Always Love You , a song that many think is about two lovers parting ways.

"That's the prettiest song I ever heard," Wagoner cried when he first heard it, her website says.

The same year, Elvis Presley was set to record a cover of the song, but Parton pulled the deal when his manager demanded half of the songwriting rights.

She cried all night at the difficult decision, and Priscilla Presley later told her that Elvis sang the song to her during their divorce.

In 1992, Whitney Houston transformed it into a now-iconic power ballad.

Parton said she was driving when she first heard the cover and had to pull over: “When I heard her go from the a cappella into the music part, I honestly thought I was going to have a heart attack, it was one of the most overwhelming things.”

Houston's cover of Parton's “sad little country song” was one of the proudest moments of her life, she said.

Parton re-recorded the song for The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, a 1982 film in which she starred and was nominated for a Golden Globe for best actress.

Another of her most famous songs was released in 1974 - Jolene.

Showing her aching vulnerability, it's about a bank clerk with flaming locks of auburn hair who flirted with her husband.

" Jolene, I'm begging of you, please don't take my man ," she pleads.

Parton said her husband, who was notoriously private, was a bit embarrassed by the song. But it was nothing serious - just a running joke between them: "I was saying, 'Hell, you're spending a lot of time at the bank. I don't believe we've got that kind of money.'"

The song has been covered by many artists including The White Stripes, Miley Cyrus and Beyoncé, who changed up the lyrics to the more ominous: " I'm warning you, don't come for my man. "

In the years to come, Dolly Parton's success only grew, with more hits, nominations and awards - she won her first Grammy in 1978 for Here You Come Again.

It was the theme song that Dolly Parton wrote for the 1980 movie 9 to 5 that fully propelled her to stardom.

Actress Jane Fonda, who produced and starred in the film about women being discriminated against in the workplace, made a deal with Parton - she'd star in the film if she could also write the theme song.

Realising her nails clicking together sounded like a typewriter, she wrote 9 to 5 while waiting around on set. Fonda said she realised straight away that it wasn't just a theme song - it was an anthem.

The film was a big success at the box office and the song won several awards, including a Golden Globe.

'I look like a woman but I think like a man'

Parton was a successful and shrewd businesswoman, and in 2022 was listed by Forbes as one of America's richest self-made women .

"I look like a woman but I think like a man. I've done business with men who think I'm as silly as I look. By the time they realise I'm not, I've got the money and gone," she once said.

Her physical appearance - the costumes, wigs, long painted nails and high heels - were merely a facade of a stereotypical “dumb blonde”. But she always said she knew she wasn't dumb "and I also know that I'm not blonde".

She had her own record label, Dolly Records, and co-owned The Dollywood Company, which manages entertainment venues, a theme park, a water park and a resort.

In 1986, she opened her Dollywood amusement park in the foothills of her beloved Smoky Mountains. As well as rollercoasters, it is home to the largest sanctuary for non-releasable bald eagles in the world. Its rehabilitation and breeding work has won awards and in 2007, the bald eagle was removed from the endangered species list.

Despite her wealth and success, Parton remained humble and supported the communities where she grew up.

Inspired by her father who couldn’t read or write, she launched the Imagination Library in 1999, which gave free books to children in Tennessee. It has since expanded to Australia, the UK, Ireland and Canada, sending out millions of free books every year.

Her non-profit organisation, The Dollywood Foundation, has funded scholarships, hospitals and donated to flood and wildfire victims.

In 2020, as the Covid-19 pandemic gripped the world, Parton donated $1m (£716,000) to the Vanderbilt University Medical Centre which helped to fund the Moderna vaccine.

How Dolly Parton became the world’s best-loved celebrity

In later years, Parton had to postpone or cancel several shows for health treatment.

In May 2026, she postponed an upcoming Las Vegas residency because of treatment for kidney stones, saying it would take some time to heal and be "stage-performance ready".

"I can't be dizzy carrying around banjos, guitars and such on five-inch heels - and you know that I'm going to be wearing them," she said in a video message.

"Not to mention all those heavy rhinestone outfits, the big hair, my big... uh, personality," she joked.

Parton spoke graciously throughout her career with humour and intelligence. She steered clear of politics, saying she didn't want to alienate half her audience.

She was a courageous and talented trailblazer for country music at a time when women were not taken seriously in the industry, especially as solo artists.

Parton said she hoped to be remembered for her songwriting and as somebody who took her work seriously, but not herself.

She once offered this advice: “Never ignore your roots, your home, or your hair."

It's guidance that she stayed true to throughout her life.

articles.title: Georgia sheriff seizes 1,800 pounds of suspected black-market marijuana shipped from California
articles.summary: A 1,800-pound black market marijuana shipment from Sacramento, California, was intercepted in Georgia, reportedly bound for Atlanta and Orlando.
articles.body: A massive shipment of 1,800 pounds of suspected black-market marijuana from California was intercepted in Georgia on Tuesday, with authorities saying the drugs were destined for Atlanta and Orlando. The shipment originated in Sacramento, where recreational marijuana is legal, according to the Butts County Sheriff’s Office. Sheriff Gary Long said about half of the marijuana was bound for Atlanta, while the rest was headed to Orlando. The sheriff’s office did not say where or how the shipment was intercepted, whether anyone was arrested or whether charges were filed. NY TIMES WALKS BACK STANCE ON MARIJUANA LEGALIZATION, ADMITS LOOSENING OF POLICIES HAS MADE COUNTRY WORSE OFF Long used the seizure to make his case that legalizing marijuana does not eliminate illegal sales. "But here is the reality: the black market isn't going away," Long said in a press release announcing the seizure. Marijuana laws vary among the three states connected to the shipment. California allows recreational marijuana, while Georgia and Florida allow marijuana only for certain medical uses. "The illegal marijuana trade does not stop at the state line," Long said. Long said Mexican drug-trafficking organizations and other criminal groups continue to move large amounts of marijuana across state lines. The sheriff’s office did not say the shipment seized Tuesday was connected to a cartel or any other criminal organization. The sheriff also argued that illegal sellers can undercut licensed marijuana businesses because they don't pay taxes or licensing fees or have to follow testing and other regulatory requirements. "As long as there is demand and money to be made, illegal dealers will continue to operate," Long said. AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING Long urged Georgia lawmakers to look closely at what has happened in states that have legalized marijuana before making changes to Georgia's laws. He pointed to California, which has changed its cannabis tax and regulatory system while continuing to fight illegal marijuana sales. He also cited past ballot initiatives filed in Colorado seeking to repeal constitutional provisions that legalized recreational marijuana, though those efforts did not reverse legalization. "That should be a warning to Georgia," Long said. "We should learn from the experiences of states that have already gone down this road instead of repeating the same mistakes and then spending years trying to fix them." Long said his statement was not meant to settle the question of whether marijuana should be legal. Instead, he argued that lawmakers need to consider how illegal sales and trafficking would fit into any changes to Georgia law.
